transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I can’t slow down—I have too many important things to take care of and I feel driven to keep doing more, day and night. It feels like if I stop for even a second, everything will fall apart, so I just have to keep moving.
During these times when you feel driven to keep moving, do you find that you need very little sleep but still feel full of energy, or are you actually exhausted but unable to sleep because of worry?

I feel completely revved up, like I'm running on electricity, and I stopped needing rest a couple of months ago. Even when my body is physically exhausted, I feel this relentless push to keep going because of the urgency of my tasks. On top of that, I keep hearing a man's voice whispering, "Don't sleep, they're counting on you," which drives me to stay awake.
Have you ever experienced periods like this in the past where you felt extremely high-energy, or times when you felt the exact opposite—very down, depressed, and empty?

I'm not really sure, to be honest, and I haven't really thought about it. Before this, I just remember having my normal, quiet routine, and right now I am just too focused on my urgent tasks to recall other times.
Have you ever been treated by a doctor or taken medication for depression, anxiety, or any other mood problems in the past?
No, I've never been treated by a doctor or taken any medication for my mood or depression in the past. I've always just managed everything on my own until things got so busy recently.
Have you ever had a period in your life lasting at least two weeks where you felt very sad, down, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

No, I don't recall ever feeling sad or losing interest in things like that. Before this, I always had a pretty steady routine, and right now I'm just too sped up and busy to think of ever feeling down.
Have you ever had a period in the past, even if it lasted just a few days, where you felt unusually happy, highly energetic, or irritable in a way that was different from your normal self?

I don't recall having any periods like this in the past. I am normally a very structured, calm person who keeps a routine of early-morning tai chi and quiet evenings. This current high-energy, overcharged state is completely new to me.
Do you feel like your thoughts are racing or moving so quickly that it is hard to keep track of them?

Yes, absolutely, my mind is racing incredibly fast! As soon as I start thinking about one thing, like my mom's blood pressure, it instantly jumps to reorganizing the med cart, fixing work schedules, and calling my sister all at the same time. It is impossible to slow down enough to finish a single thought before the next one hits me.
Do you feel like you have been given special powers, extraordinary abilities, or a unique mission that other people don't have?

I absolutely feel a unique, critical responsibility that nobody else seems to understand. I know in my gut that only I can catch the mistakes and prevent a disaster to keep my patients and parents safe. It is so frustrating that my husband and coworkers don't see how necessary my constant vigilance is and just try to get in my way.
Have you recently started any new medications, used any over-the-counter supplements, or taken any substances like stimulants?
No, I haven't started any new medications or taken any over-the-counter supplements lately. I also don't use any stimulants or other substances at all.
How has this constant rush, the racing thoughts, and the voice you hear affected your ability to work, manage your daily life, or get along with your family?

It has caused so much friction because people just don't understand—I've been written up at work for arguing with doctors, and my husband says he can't reason with me and is sleeping in the guest room. On top of that, I've been skipping my own meals and doctor appointments because I am just too busy micromanaging everyone else's care. I don't have time to worry about myself when everyone's lives are on the line!

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a first-time, distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally increased energy, lasting for approximately two months. She exhibits classic manic symptoms including a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, and psychomotor agitation, resulting in severe functional impairment (disciplinary action at work and marital discord). Additionally, she displays psychotic features, including auditory hallucinations (a whispering voice telling her not to sleep) and grandiose delusions (believing she has a unique, critical responsibility to prevent a disaster). Since there is no prior history of manic or depressive episodes, a single manic episode with psychotic symptoms (F30.2) is the most appropriate diagnosis, with bipolar affective disorder (F31.2) and schizoaffective disorder (F25.0) as primary differentials.
